title: US's AI task force sets path for study and reviews, leader tells CNBC
source_used: Bloomberg (read in the Yahoo Finance copy) and PYMNTS, which relays Bloomberg and CNBC; Reuters preview of the meeting read on AOL
key_facts: President Donald Trump's AI task force, which he calls the Super Intelligence Task Force, held its first meeting on Thursday 15 Oct 2026.
It agreed to address risks in cybersecurity, biosecurity and 'model control and accountability', according to a White House account of the meeting.
It will commission a report on those and other concerns from the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
It will develop protocols for AI labs to give the government early warnings and systemized notifications of breaches, hacks, jailbreaks and other issues.
It plans a law enforcement and consumer protection coordination committee including the Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission and other agencies.
The White House said the group did not discuss any new laws or rules; Trump has rejected calls for more regulation and brokered a voluntary agreement with industry that uses outside auditors.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, who leads the group, told CNBC on Friday 16 Oct 2026 that the meeting was 'very good' and that the US must stay ahead of China, Russia, Iran and North Korea on AI.
The Wall Street Journal reported on 3 Oct 2026 that the White House gave the task force 120 days to report on the risks and rewards of AI.
quote_evidence: President Donald Trump's artificial intelligence task force in its first meeting agreed on Thursday to address risks related to cybersecurity, biosecurity and "model control and accountability" as fears rise over the potential dangers posed by the technology.
The task force, according to the White House account, did not discuss any new laws or rules
The Chinese, the Russians, the Iranians, the North Koreans all have significant technical capability
why_it_matters_hint: The White House's AI panel has set a study-and-warning agenda but no new rules, which matters as AI becomes a midterm election issue.
